issues.legal_issue: An application to reject a plaint must be decided from the plaint read as a whole together with documents relied on by the plaintiff, without relying on the defendant’s disputed merits, and the plaint must be rejected when those materials show no cause of action or a legal bar.
material_facts: The purchasers sought rejection of the plaint on the grounds that it disclosed no cause of action and was barred by limitation.
The sale deed was filed with and relied on in the plaint, and its recitals acknowledged receipt of the full consideration and transfer of possession.
The courts below relied on the plaint and the sale deed in rejecting the plaint.
issues.conclusion: The courts below properly considered the plaint and its supporting documents and rejected it at the threshold; the Supreme Court affirmed that result.
issues.legal_principle: Order VII Rules 11(a) and 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure require rejection where the plaint discloses no cause of action or appears from its statements to be barred by law. Under Order VII Rule 14(1), documents relied on by the plaintiff and filed with the plaint may be considered, and a document forming the basis of the plaint is treated as part of it. The court assumes the plaint’s factual allegations to be true and reads them as a whole, but may reject a sham or illusory claim. The defendant’s written statement and disputed merits are irrelevant at this stage. The remedy is mandatory when a ground is made out and may be used at any stage. The Court relied on Azhar Hussain v. Rajiv Gandhi, Liverpool & London S.P. & I Assn. Ltd. v. M.V. Sea Success I, Hardesh Ores (P.) Ltd. v. Hede & Co., Sopan Sukhdeo Sable v. Assistant Charity Commissioner, Saleem Bhai v. State of Maharashtra, T. Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal, I.T.C. Ltd. v. Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal, and Madanuri Sri Ramachandra Murthy v. Syed Jalal.

rule.if: plaint_rejection_proceeding and plaintiff_relies_on_supporting_documents and (plaint_discloses_no_cause_of_action or plaint_shows_legal_bar)

predicates.plaint_rejection_proceeding: A party asks the court to reject a plaint before the suit proceeds to a full trial.
predicates.plaint_relies_on_supporting_documents: The plaintiff relies on documents filed with the plaint that form the basis of the claim.
predicates.plaint_discloses_no_cause_of_action: The plaint, read as a whole and with its supporting documents, does not disclose facts establishing a right to the relief sought.
predicates.plaint_shows_legal_bar: The plaint and its supporting documents show that a law bars the suit.
predicates.plaint_must_be_rejected: The court rejects the plaint without proceeding to a full trial.

issues.definition: When a rejection proceeding is brought and the plaint and its supporting documents disclose no cause of action or show a legal bar, the plaint must be rejected.

issues.legal_issue: Non-payment of some or all of the price does not invalidate a completed sale where the parties intended to transfer ownership for a price paid or promised.
material_facts: The plaintiffs admitted executing and registering the sale deed and sought its cancellation on the ground that most of the consideration represented by cheques had not been paid.
The deed recited that the full consideration had been paid and that possession had been transferred.
The plaint sought cancellation of the deed rather than merely recovery of the alleged unpaid balance.
issues.conclusion: Even assuming the alleged non-payment was true, it did not entitle the plaintiffs to cancel the sale deed; they could pursue other remedies to recover the unpaid consideration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 defines a sale as a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised, or part paid and part promised. Actual payment of the whole price at execution is not essential to completion of a sale. Once the deed is executed and registered with an intention to transfer ownership, non-payment of part of the price does not undo the transfer or justify cancellation. The Court relied on Vidyadhar v. Manikrao.

rule.if: suit_seeks_cancellation_of_sale and conveyance_executed_and_registered and parties_intended_to_transfer_ownership and price_was_paid_or_promised and price_allegedly_remains_unpaid

predicates.suit_seeks_cancellation_of_sale: The plaintiff brings a suit seeking cancellation of a conveyance of property.
predicates.conveyance_executed_and_registered: The parties executed and registered a document conveying the property.
predicates.parties_intended_to_transfer_ownership: The parties intended the conveyance to transfer ownership to the purchaser.
predicates.price_was_paid_or_promised: The transfer was made for a price paid, promised, or partly paid and partly promised.
predicates.price_allegedly_remains_unpaid: The plaintiff alleges that some or all of the agreed price was not paid.
predicates.nonpayment_does_not_invalidate_sale: The alleged non-payment does not invalidate the completed sale or entitle the plaintiff to cancel it.

issues.definition: If parties intended and completed a registered transfer for a price paid or promised, an allegation that the price remains unpaid does not make the sale invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A suit to cancel a conveyance is time-barred when the facts supporting cancellation were known when the conveyance was executed and the suit is brought after the applicable limitation period; later discovery of a document index does not create a new accrual date.
material_facts: The plaintiffs alleged that the bulk of the consideration had not been paid when the last cheques were delivered and the registered sale deed was executed.
The deed identified the cheques and expressly acknowledged receipt of the full consideration.

The plaintiffs alleged that they discovered the fraud only when they obtained an index and a copy of the deed years later, but they did not complain or seek recovery of the alleged unpaid amount during the intervening period.
The suit seeking cancellation was filed beyond three years from the alleged non-payment and execution of the deed.
issues.conclusion: The right to sue arose when the alleged non-payment occurred, not when the plaintiffs later obtained the index; the cancellation claim was barred by limitation under Article 59.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(j) and 3 of the Limitation Act, 1963 define the prescribed period and require dismissal of a suit instituted after it. Articles 58 and 59 prescribe three years for the relevant declaration or cancellation claim, running from when the right to sue first accrues or the facts entitling cancellation first become known. A later or successive event does not restart limitation where the right to sue first accrued earlier. The court examines the plaint to identify when the right to seek relief arose. The Court relied on Khatri Hotels Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, State of Punjab v. Gurdev Singh, and Raghwendra Sharan Singh v. Ram Prasanna Singh.

predicates.suit_seeks_cancellation_of_instrument: The plaintiff brings a suit seeking cancellation of an instrument.
predicates.cancellation_facts_known_when_claim_firs: The plaintiff knew the facts alleged to justify cancellation when the asserted injury or non-performance first occurred.
predicates.suit_filed_beyond_applicable_limitation_: The plaintiff filed the suit after the limitation period applicable to the claim had expired.
predicates.later_discovery_is_only_of_document_inde: The plaintiff relies on later receipt of an index or copy of a document, although the underlying facts supporting the claim had already occurred and were known.
predicates.cancellation_claim_is_time_barred: The court holds that the cancellation claim was brought too late.

issues.definition: A cancellation claim is time-barred when its supporting facts were known at the first accrual of the right to sue, the suit was filed after the applicable limitation period, and later discovery concerns only an index of the document.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge to a subsequent conveyance cannot proceed when the underlying conveyance claim is rejected and the plaintiff alleges no independent basis for relief against the subsequent purchasers.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought cancellation of both the original conveyance and a later conveyance to subsequent purchasers.
The claim to cancel the original conveyance was rejected for disclosing no sustainable right to cancellation and for being time-barred.
The plaintiffs made no independent allegation against the subsequent purchasers.
issues.conclusion: Once the claim concerning the original conveyance was rejected, the related claim to cancel the subsequent conveyance could not be entertained.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that, in the circumstances of this case, rejection of the claim concerning the original conveyance also precluded the derivative challenge to the later conveyance where no independent basis for relief against the subsequent purchasers was pleaded.

predicates.suit_challenges_subsequent_conveyance: The plaintiff seeks relief against a conveyance made by the original purchaser to later purchasers.
predicates.underlying_conveyance_claim_rejected: The plaintiff’s claim challenging the conveyance through which the original purchaser acquired the property has been rejected.
predicates.no_independent_basis_against_subsequent_: The plaintiff pleads no independent ground for relief against the later purchasers.
predicates.subsequent_conveyance_challenge_cannot_b: The court does not entertain the derivative challenge to the subsequent conveyance.

issues.definition: A challenge to a later conveyance cannot be entertained when the underlying conveyance claim has been rejected and no independent basis for relief against the later purchasers is pleaded.
